coverage.note: Built from headlines and RSS descriptions published between 10:00 on Saturday and 10:00 on Tuesday Copenhagen time, from 131 feeds at sixteen publishers, all polled successfully. Danish outlets decide what is news; international titles are linked where they cover the same story. Nothing else was read.

copy.headline: Russian frigate fires flares at Danish helicopter off Gedser

extended.text: A Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish Fennec helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, during what the Defence Command describes as routine photo documentation of the ship. The Foreign Ministry has summoned Russia's ambassador.
Defence minister Jeppe Bruus calls the situation serious. There had been no prior communication with the frigate as far as he knows.

The incident is 'unfortunately not surprising', Mette Frederiksen said in a written statement on Tuesday. It shows Russia testing and challenging NATO, the behaviour of an 'aggressive and assertive Russia'.
Politicians across the parties have united behind a joint message to Moscow, Jyllands-Posten reports from its live coverage, and foreign minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen responded on Tuesday morning.
Both the frigate and the helicopter had every right to be where they were, Kristina Siig, professor of maritime law at Aalborg University, tells Ritzau.
The Defence Ministry's statement landed at 23:02 on Monday night. Michael Jarlner, Politiken's international commentator, reads the affair as part of a new and risky pattern.

copy.headline: Supreme Court blocks Trump's bid to restrict postal voting

standard.text: The US Supreme Court on Monday refused to let the postal service enforce stricter rules on mail-in ballots, so states can send ballots by post as normal ahead of the midterms.
Trump, a long-standing opponent of postal voting, had signed the order in late March. The justices he appointed helped deliver what Politiken calls a decisive defeat.

copy.headline: AI shares slide as Trump calls safety warnings a 'sick conspiracy'

standard.text: Warnings from the heads of the leading US AI companies that development is moving too fast pushed US stocks down on Monday, with Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron the heaviest weights. European AI-related shares fell too.

Trump sees no need for the safety framework the executives called for. He describes a 'sick conspiracy' against AI and data centres that only China could welcome, and says a 'strong and smart president' will rein the technology in.

Germany, speaking for Europe, does not believe in limiting AI, TV 2 reports. Critics tell Berlingske the executives are 'wolves in sheep's clothing', and a former 'AI czar' warns against taking their motives as altruistic.
Danes' expectations of AI have plunged in two years, a survey shows; bad experiences appear to have fed the scepticism, experts tell Politiken.

copy.headline: Sweden's Centre Party rules out Kristersson as coalition talks begin

standard.text: The Centre Party wants a government with the Social Democrats and will not cooperate with Ulf Kristersson's Moderates, it said on Monday.
That leaves its leader, Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, a front-line politician only since November 2025, in a position Politiken compares to the Moderates' in Denmark.

Kristersson has a bold plan to hold on to power despite the blocs standing far closer than expected, Jyllands-Posten reports. Forming a government may take a month or more, and a new election cannot be ruled out.
Swedish authorities found no sign of foreign interference in the election.
